questions.prompt: An agent rewrote your analysis script and the results look wrong. Which command returns tracked files to your last commit?
questions.explain: Restore reverts tracked files to the last commit immediately; no new commit is needed.

options.misconception: Committing records the broken state as a new snapshot; it does not revert your working files.
Pop re-applies earlier stashed changes on top of your files; it does not discard the agent's edits.
Staging records the broken state; it does not undo it.

questions.prompt: When should you commit a snapshot?
questions.explain: A snapshot only protects you if it exists before the mistake happens.

options.text: Before letting the agent make changes

options.misconception: Committing afterwards snapshots the possibly broken state, so you lose your undo point.

options.text: Only when the project is finished
options.misconception: A snapshot only protects you if it exists before the mistake happens.

questions.prompt: The agent made a new file `scratch.py` and also edited `analysis.py`. You run `git restore .`. What state are you in?
questions.explain: Restore reverts tracked files. New files stay, so check `git status` for leftovers.

options.text: analysis.py is reverted; scratch.py remains, untracked
Both files are reverted, scratch.py is deleted too
options.misconception: restore only reverts tracked files. New untracked files stay until you remove them.

options.text: Nothing changes until you also run git add on the files
options.misconception: restore acts on your working files immediately; no commit is needed.
